Everything in v8.0.0 was reviewed afterwards, line by line, and this release is what that turned up: fifty-two confirmed defects, fixed. The pattern behind most of them is worth naming, because it is not carelessness - in nearly every case the correct guard already existed a few files away, often with a comment describing exactly the damage that then happened where it was missing. A schedule that ignored its own off switch. An exclusion assistant that counted the files it was excluding. A restore button that asked no questions. Alongside those, the cross-site write path is closed, and three issues reported since 8.0.0 are fixed.

## ⚡ Improved

- **A Fleet peer card stays open ([#179](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/179)).** Collapsed, a peer card shows little more than a name, an address and a poll badge - the protection scorecard is the content, and it closed again on every visit. The open state is now remembered in your browser: open one card and every card is open next time you come back.

- **The language picker, and every other dropdown, can be used from the keyboard.** The list panel never moved focus, so opening it with Enter left you on the button and the next Tab jumped past all 42 languages to the following control. Focus now lands on the selected option, the arrow keys and Home/End walk the list, and closing returns focus to where you were.

- **The colour picker can be used without a mouse.** The saturation square and the hue bar were plain surfaces with no keyboard handling at all, which was a step back from the native colour input they replaced - the accent swatch at least kept its eight presets, the rainbow palette had no way in. Both are proper sliders now: arrows nudge, Shift and Page Up/Down take a bigger step, Home and End go to the ends, and a screen reader is told the actual values.

- **A disabled button can still tell you what it is.** For the icon-only controls the tooltip is the only thing naming them, and a disabled control emits no hover events - so the explanation disappeared at exactly the moment you wanted it, while the control sat there dead.

- **Off-site destinations are tested with their own credentials.** The tamper test resolved credentials once and reused them for every destination, so a destination using a named credential set was probed with the shared ones. That never produced a false green - an authentication failure is deliberately treated as "no verdict" - but it did mean those destinations were silently never verified at all.

## 🐛 Fixed

- **The protection status ignored Backup Everything ([#177](https://github.com/junkerderprovinz/bombvault/issues/177)).** With the per-domain schedules off and the whole-server pass doing the work, the dashboard reported "Not scheduled" for containers, VMs, flash and folders while they were being backed up nightly. The label was the visible half. The same reading also drives the overdue watchdog, where "no schedule" means "no expectation" - so a server backed up entirely through the pass had no overdue alerting on any domain, and nothing said so. Both now count the pass, and where a domain has a schedule of its own as well, the shorter of the two applies. The weekly digest's off-site staleness check had the same blind spot.

- **A row in the recovery list could restore without asking.** One click on the small restore badge started an in-place restore over live appdata or VM disks, with no confirmation, while the "Restore all" button in the same card asked first. It asks now.

- **Backup Everything ignored the domain switches.** Every other part of BombVault reads them - the protection status, the watchdog, the drills, and the interface, which hides a switched-off domain's whole tab. The pass ran them anyway, which hurt in both directions: on a host with no Unraid flash the flash step failed on every single pass and failed the parent run with it, which is the one signal the feature exists to produce; and with the flash domain switched off on Unraid it would create a repository nobody asked for.

- **And it charged for domains with nothing to do.** On a machine with no VMs and no folder sets, every pass pinged a green "0 of 0 items succeeded" at your dead-man's switch - turning a check that had gone red back to green for a pass that touched nothing - and paid for a full prune and an off-site repository open, twice, for it.

- **Switching a domain off did not stop its schedule.** Turn a domain off after setting a schedule and the nightly run kept going, container stop/start, prune and off-site replication included, while the dashboard, the watchdog and the drill set all reported that domain as off and its tab was gone from the interface. It said off everywhere you could look, and ran anyway.

- **A weekly schedule on several weekdays was read as a daily one.** "Weekly, Saturday and Sunday" was measured as a one-day window instead of six, so the domain went to warning every Monday and overdue every Tuesday, and sent a weekly "expected every 1d" alert about a schedule that was running exactly as configured. The same number also drives the tamper, off-site, drill and digest windows, which were quietly impatient for the same reason.

- **Two settings saves could wipe stored secrets.** If the read that fills the notification or cloud card failed - a restart, a moment's network trouble - the card stayed empty and the next click saved that emptiness over everything: SMTP password, Matrix token, per-domain healthchecks. The toast said "Saved". Neither card will save now until a read has actually succeeded, and says so on screen.

- **A bulk restore could reach containers the filter had hidden.** Selecting containers, switching the filter, and pressing restore ran in-place restores on rows that were no longer on screen.

- **The exclusion assistant counted the files it excludes.** With a line like `*.log` stored, every log file's bytes still flowed into its folder's total, so a folder that is 90% logs was proposed at its full size - recommending you exclude a folder on the strength of bytes you had already excluded. A pattern with a wildcard in a path, like `/config/*/Cache`, matched nothing at all for the same reason.

- **The exclusion scan died when whoever started it closed their tab.** The scan is shared between everyone waiting for it, and it ran on the request of whoever happened to arrive first. It also read as "nothing left to exclude" when it had produced no answer at all, rather than as a failure.

- **A stop-list emptied itself between screen updates.** Ticking containers under "stop other containers" and then triggering any refresh silently saved a list without them.

- **Two pages could never clear an error banner.** A red banner from one transient failure stayed above the correctly reloaded list for as long as the page was open, and hid the empty state and the "no matches" hint with it.

- **Two recovery actions rolled back changes made elsewhere.** Attaching a repository or restoring the configuration saved a full copy of the settings as they were when the page loaded, so anything changed meanwhile from another tab, another device or a settings import was quietly reverted, cadences and retention included.

- **A cancelled run was reported as "Skipped".** The dashboard described a different event than the one you had just caused.

- **The self-backup schedule forgot its cadence.** Switching it off and on again gave you "daily at 02:00" back rather than the weekly time you had set, with a success toast either way.

- **A per-item schedule could be typed and lost.** Set a cadence and switch tab within a second, and it was gone with no message - the auto-save is the only thing that stores it, and it was discarded rather than completed.

- **Two schedule reloads at once registered every domain twice.** Saving settings twice in quick succession could leave the scheduler running each nightly backup twice over the same repository.

- **A backup recorded with a wrong clock sorted last forever.** A timestamp in the future - a dead CMOS battery, or the moments before the clock is corrected at boot - can never be beaten by a later, correct run, so that container drifted to the end of the queue permanently.

- **A hook that hung left its children running,** and its output could grow without limit for five minutes. A hook is usually a small pipeline, and only the outer shell was being stopped.

- **A crash in the scheduled whole-server pass left it showing as running** in the activity log and run history until the next restart.

- **Two database repairs.** An installation upgraded along one particular path could end up unable to read its own settings at all; and a pass that ended in a crash was recorded as having completed, which made the "every N days" gate skip the following interval.

- **The Fleet peer version printed a doubled "v"** ("vv8.0.0"), and the fleet sweep showed up in the activity log as "Backup (fleet)".

- **A tooltip or dropdown taller than the space below it ran off the bottom of the screen** instead of being moved back inside it, and the time picker never returned keyboard focus when it closed.

## 🔒 Security

- **Cross-site writes are refused.** With no login password set - the documented trusted-LAN default - BombVault deliberately does not authenticate, on the assumption that an attacker has to be on your network. A page on the public internet does not: an ordinary HTML form in your own browser could reach a LAN address and change settings, with no preflight and no cookie needed. That was enough to redirect every notification, or to set the Backup Everything hook commands, which run as shell commands in a container holding the Docker socket. Requests that change something must now declare JSON and must not be marked cross-site by the browser, and the settings import carries the same guard. **If you drive this API from a script, send `Content-Type: application/json`** - anything else is now refused with 415. The interface and fleet-to-fleet traffic already did.

- **A stored secret stays with its own destination.** The notification test filled a blank Matrix token or SMTP password in from encrypted storage while taking the destination from the request, so a request naming its own server with a blank token had the real one attached and sent there - a way to read back a secret the interface never shows, dressed up as a connection test. A stored secret is now only ever filled in for the destination it was saved for, and changing the destination asks you to enter it again rather than silently blanking it.

- **`GET /api/settings` no longer hands out the hook commands and off-site repository addresses in full.** A useful hook carries its secret in its URL, and a restic address can carry a user and password.

## 🌐 Translations

- Nine new strings across all 42 languages: the confirmation before a row restore, the protection status naming what covers a domain, the accessible names for the colour picker's two sliders and for the selection checkboxes, the "cancelled" run state, and the activity log's names for the fleet and receiver sweeps.

## 📝 Notes

- One finding is documented rather than fixed, on purpose. A schedule set to a wall-clock time behaves oddly across a daylight-saving change: the spring day where that time does not exist is skipped, and the autumn day where it happens twice fires twice. This was measured against the scheduling library rather than assumed - and so was the fix that was proposed for it, which turns out to change nothing at all. Rather than ship something that looks like a repair and is not, the code now records what actually happens and what a real fix would take. A one-off missed or repeated nightly run is visible in the run history either way.
